transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-04-01 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Heliostat CTO), Ravi Kapoor (Head Infra), Tasha Osei (ML Eng), Liam Murphy (Procurement)
Links shared: Redwood POC bench template: https://redwood.internal/bench/heliostat-poc (internal link), Example replay tool repo: https://git.internal/heliostat-replay (note)

Summary: quick scoping to align on success metrics, traffic signature (QPS, concurrency, input/output token distribution), bench plan and timeline. Customer wants production-like replay and clear pass/fail SLA for latency and correctness.

Topics covered: success criteria, QPS/concurrency envelope, token length distribution, warm vs cold KV cache behavior, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, data residency and SOC2/KMS questions, timeline for pilot runs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira: Cool, uh thanks everyone for carving time today. We want to run through the POC checklist then nail the workload signature so Ethan can design the benchmark harness. Maya, do you want to start with a quick overview of what you expect from the pilot?
[00:18] Maya: Yeah sure, um thanks Samira. So our main goal is to validate latency SLO at scale — we have two primary flows: a synchronous chat-type assistant behind our support product and a longer async batch summarization pipeline. The chat flow is the priority, about 60% of calls.
[00:35] Ravi: And I'll add, security is a hard constraint, we need VPC peering for any dedicated runs and KMS keys for anything stored. Also we have to get procurement sign-off so cost estimates matter.
[00:48] Ethan: Got it. When you say latency SLO, can you quantify the target p50/p95/p99 for the chat?
[00:56] Maya: Target is p95 < 350ms for the short prompts, p99 < 800ms ideally. For the summarization it's looser, p95 < 2s. These are user-facing.
[01:12] Samira: Good, makes sense. For the POC we usually run against an observed QPS envelope and a replay of real requests to catch token mix. Tasha, can you talk about token lengths and payloads?
[01:23] Tasha: Yeah, rough distribution: input tokens mostly 8-60 tokens, median ~22. Output tokens for chat are typically 20-120, median ~45. For the batch summarizer task output can be 300-1,200 tokens in some edge cases, average ~420. There's also a small percent — maybe 5% — of very long outputs for certain legal docs.
[01:47] Ethan: That distribution is super helpful. We usually split tests into short/medium/long buckets to emulate concurrency and KV cache hit ratios. Do you have conversation prefixes / system messages that are reused across requests? That affects prefix caching.
[02:03] Tasha: Yes, we have a persistent system prompt that's about 60 tokens and then user messages vary. The prefix is included maybe 80% of requests, sometimes omitted for terse queries.
[02:18] Maya: Also context windows vary; the assistant keeps a 2-turn context on chat, so average total tokens per request is higher than just input tokens.
[02:28] Ethan: Good nuance. For sizing we'll need sample histogram files for: inter-arrival (QPS), per-request input/out token counts, and concurrency peaks. Can you share 7 days of anonymized telemetry?
[02:40] Maya: We can extract that, yeah. We want to strip user PII, obviously. We'll aim to send csv histograms.
[02:49] Samira: Great. On the infrastructure side, do you expect spikes or predictable bursts?
[02:55] Ravi: Spikes. Our traffic is diurnal but also has bursts when our dashboard jobs run and during ticket surges. Peak bursts are usually 10x baseline for short periods — like 120s windows.
[03:10] Ethan: Ok we'll include burst scenarios. Typical POC plan: 1) replay-run to verify latency SLOs at baseline QPS and then at peak burst 2) stress run to push concurrency to saturation and measure tail-latency 3) cold-start tests and KV-cache-warm runs. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and token-cost per request.
[03:29] Liam: From procurement side we need an estimate of expected monthly token consumption to compare hosted vs dedicated. Are you able to project that from the replay?
[03:38] Samira: Yes — once we have the replay traffic we can give estimated token-month and a few cost scenarios: hosted pay-as-you-go, and a dedicated commit with expected unit improvements when using batching/cache. We'll produce a short cost delta sheet.
[03:52] Maya: One question — for accurate latency we need the bench runner to preserve real network RTTs. Can Redwood simulate client RTT or should we run in our VPC?
[04:01] Ethan: We can do both. For hosted tests we'll add a configurable synthetic latency distribution to the runner. For dedicated/VPC tests it's best to run from your VPC or a peered test subnet so the network shape is realistic.
[04:12] Ravi: We'll set up a temporary peering window if needed.
[04:16] Samira: Perfect. On model side, do you already have a model family selected? Open LLM or a fine-tuned variant?
[04:23] Tasha: We're using a fine-tuned Llama-derivative internally but open to using a close match for benchmark runs. We want to ensure tokenization differences aren't skewing results.
[04:34] Ethan: Tokenization can matter. If you can provide a small set of exact requests and expected output lengths from your model, we can align tokenizer and also run a quick per-token latency check.
[04:45] Tasha: I'll include sample payloads in the export.
[04:49] Maya: On success criteria — aside from p95/p99 — we want determinism checks for generation fidelity: a small set of golden prompts we expect exact or near-exact responses for. If you regress on those we fail.
[05:03] Samira: We'll wire in a simple rouge-like check or exact-match tolerance for the golden set. We'll capture quality metrics in the bench report.
[05:11] Maya: Also we require audit logs for inference calls for compliance.
[05:17] Samira: Understood. Redwood provides request-level audit logs in the console for Dedicated/Private; hosted has configurable retention. I'll share the SOC2 packet and logging doc.
[05:27] Ethan: Quick technical question: are you expecting KV-cache to be warm during chat bursts? That can change p99 dramatically.
[05:33] Tasha: For typical customer traffic cache warms gradually; but for sudden spikes many requests will be cold. We want both scenarios tested.
[05:41] Ethan: We'll run with a cold start sweep then a warm steady-state run. We'll also measure effective cache hit rate with prefixes.
[05:49] Ravi: For dedicated deployment, is there an expected autoscale behavior? We need to know how Redwood handles queueing vs rejecting under overload.
[05:57] Samira: Our Dedicated product has configurable autoscale policies and burst capacity. For the POC we can show both modes: strict SLO with queueing up to a threshold and a degraded mode with best-effort. We'll surface drop counts in report.
[06:11] Liam: Procurement will need an NDA and a draft MSA if we proceed after the POC. Is Redwood OK with a typical 60-day eval MSA?
[06:20] Samira: Yes we can share the MSA; we usually have a POC addendum and standard SLA for Dedicated pilots. I'll send the legal packet.
[06:29] Maya: Back to workload — concurrency: our app layer keeps up to ~200 concurrent websocket sessions but actual model concurrency usually ~40 concurrent model requests sustained with spikes to 180 for the 2-minute windows.
[06:43] Ethan: That concurrency shape will strongly influence batching benefits. We'll capture throughput per GPU and token-per-second metrics.
[06:52] Samira: For the bench design, Ethan will propose a run plan with these phases: baseline steady-state at 40 concurrent, ramp to 180 over 60s, 2-minute peak hold, then cooldown; repeated for short/medium/long token profiles. Does that match expectations?
[07:08] Tasha: Yes, please also include a spiral test where you gradually increase sequence length for the long outputs to see comp penalties.
[07:16] Ethan: We'll add that. For measurement we'll export p50/p95/p99 latencies, upstream queueing time, GPU utilization, token/sec, and per-request token cost estimate.
[07:28] Ravi: We also want to measure effect of quantization—we plan to run a quantized variant in prod. Can Redwood serve quantized model builds?
[07:36] Ethan: Yes our runtime supports int8/4-bit paths and different quantization profiles. For the POC, if you want we can run the unquantized baseline and a matched quantized build to compare latency and throughput.
[07:48] Maya: That would be valuable. Anything we should prepare about model artifacts?
[07:53] Ethan: If you can export a container or weights tarball, we can load a non-public model in Dedicated/private test clusters; for hosted we can test a compatible open checkpoint. We'll need model config and tokenizer.
[08:05] Tasha: We can export weights under NDA.
[08:09] Samira: Great. Timeline — propose we: 1) data export and replay config 2) Redwood sets up replay runner and smoke test 3) benchmark runs week of Apr 14 4) debrief and sizing recommendation Apr 21. Is that aggressive?
[08:25] Maya: That timeline works if we can get the data to you by Apr 4.
[08:29] Samira: Ok so target data delivery Apr 4, smoke test Apr 7-9, full bench Apr 14-16, debrief Apr 21. We'll mark that in next_steps.
[08:39] Liam: On pricing estimates for procurement, can Redwood provide a sample TCO calc with hosted vs dedicated and a mid-tier commit example?
[08:49] Samira: Yes we'll produce a 3-scenario cost comparison. We'll annotate assumptions and show tokens/month and expected cost/unit.
[08:58] Ethan: A technical caveat — model warm-up and KV cache priming can shave 15-30% off p95 in some workloads; we will show both cold and primed curves so you can see realistic production ops.
[09:10] Tasha: Also instrument memory use for long outputs; we saw OOMs in our internal experiments on x86 inference when sequence length hit 1,500.
[09:19] Ethan: We'll include memory/GPU mem metrics and OOM counts.
[09:25] Maya: For success gating, proposal: pass if p95 <= 350ms for short profile and p99 < 1s for short profile across 90% of runs, plus no regressions on golden prompts and acceptable cost delta (within X% of our target). We need Redwood to propose exact gating.
[09:46] Samira: We'll formalize gating in the bench matrix — include p50/p95/p99, golden-prompt pass rate, cost per 1M tokens, and error/log anomalies threshold.
[09:57] Ravi: About observability — we need token-level billing and per-route dashboards. Does Redwood expose those?
[10:04] Samira: Yes console has per-route token breakdowns and tracing hooks. For Dedicated we can ship logs to your ELK or Datadog.
[10:11] Maya: Can you also include request sampling for exact payloads in traces?
[10:16] Samira: Yes configurable sampling; for PII reasons we'll keep payloads masked unless you request exact captures under NDA.
[10:24] Ethan: Quick note on replay fidelity — two artifacts are helpful: 1) a CSV of request timestamps, input token count, output token target (if you have a recorded response), and 2) a small set of raw sample payloads for golden checks.
[10:36] Tasha: We'll prepare both.
[10:39] Samira: Great. Other concerns?
[10:42] Maya: On multi-region — we want to understand routing policies if our users are EU-heavy. Does Redwood support region pinning?
[10:49] Samira: Yes region-aware routing and model pinning are supported. For the POC we'll keep traffic in us-west but can test EU routing in a follow-up.
[10:59] Ravi: For security, can we do an engineering security review?
[11:02] Samira: We can schedule an SKIP — sorry, a security deep-dive; Ethan can join with our security eng. We'll add it as a follow-up.
[11:12] Ethan: I'll coordinate with security.
[11:15] Liam: Procurement question — if we go dedicated, is there a minimum commit length?
[11:19] Samira: Typical commitments are 3/6/12 months. For pilots there's often a month-to-month pilot credit arrangement; we can discuss.
[11:28] Maya: Ok, sounds good. One more technical: can Redwood simulate mixed workloads (chat + batch) concurrently in the runner? We need to ensure batch jobs don't starve chat traffic.
[11:38] Ethan: Yes the runner supports mixed cohorts with route-level weights and QoS shaping so we can enforce priority for chat. We'll include a QoS config in the bench plan.
[11:49] Tasha: Ensure you measure tail-latency under mixed load — that's our biggest concern.
[11:53] Ethan: Will do.
[11:55] Samira: Ok, quick recap of next steps and owners: Samira send legal and SOC2, Ethan send bench runner and matrix, Maya/Tasha send anonymized telemetry and samples, Ravi confirm peering window, Liam track procurement milestones. We'll follow up with calendar invites for smoke and benchmark windows.
[12:18] Maya: Thanks all, that covers it.
[12:22] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll email the checklist and confirm target dates.
[12:27] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: Automated transcript curation present; some mis-IDs of proper nouns (e.g., "Llama-derivative" may appear as "Loma-derivative"), occasional filler words retained.

- replay runner repo + runbook
- smoke test summary and full bench report with p50/p95/p99, GPU metrics, token cost projection, golden-prompt fidelity checks
